searchText: Hey peeps, hope everyone is well. Just had a quick question in regards to the Ethereum modular architecture roadmap and the security implications: So my understanding of the direction Ethereum is headed in is this: Keep consensus layer at L1, extract the execution layer to L2, and eventually extract some of the data layer (to a 3rd party?), i.e. 'history/state expiry'. - Is this correct? And if yes, then doesn't that decrease the security of Ethereum if we're delegating execution to a relatively centralized body of L2's (L2s are essentially 'companies', no? Perhaps they're Ethereum-aligned companies, but companies nonetheless?), and delegating storage to a potentially less decentralized platform. That is to say, does this modular approach create added points of failure, since the three pillars are no longer unified and self-contained in a given L1 node? This reduces censorship resistance if the L2s people move to aren't censorship resistant. It is possible to build censorship resistant L2s though. Unfortunately, all current L2s are censorable. 😖 Generally sharding greatly decreases security as a trade off Current eth is probably the most secure it’ll ever be. Though I guess if hashrate was more spread out it would be even more secure. Danksharding is only sharding for a subset of definitions of sharding. 😄 Which means it doesn't suffer from the security tradeoffs of full sharding. oh, nice! Okay, looking forward to the education of dank sharding to the general public and how it preserves security! <@!301186049323958275> one quick follow up - given that L2's are censorable, are you worried at all about the future security of Ethereum and its ability to serve as a reliable (i.e. resistant to nation state and cyber terrorist attacks) base layer for a new decentralized economy? Ethereum will remain censorship resistant, even if people build censorable things on top of it. are you omitting Fuel for some reason? what? how does sharding reduce security Sharding violates the "Don't trust, verify" rule. Not arguing against sharding just acknowledging that it reduces security in return for the benefits. are you talking about weak subjectivity? I'll be honest, I lack the knowledge and understanding to debate this. From my understanding each validator is not verifying all shards and instead trusts others to have done so? This article appears to express some of my concerns https://medium.com/hackernoon/sharding-centralizes-ethereum-by-selling-you-scaling-in-disguised-as-scaling-out-266c136fc55d
